content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published a guide titled Planning and Implementing Palliative Care Services: A Guide for Programme Managers. This document provides detailed guidance on the organization, administration, and utilization of palliative care services, including hospice care, health planning, and the integration of palliative care into national health programs. The publication is intended to support health program managers at various levels—national, provincial, or district—who are responsible for noncommunicable diseases, infectious disease programs, or other technical areas where palliative care is essential. Palliative care is defined as an approach that enhances the quality of life for patients, both adults and children, and their families who are dealing with life-threatening illnesses. It focuses on the prevention and relief of suffering through early identification, accurate assessment, and treatment of pain and other physical, psychological, social, or spiritual problems. Palliative care promotes dignity, quality of life, and adaptation to progressive illnesses, using the best available evidence. Palliative care for children is a specialized field that involves the active, comprehensive care of the child’s body, mind, and spirit, while also providing support to the family. It begins at the time of diagnosis and continues regardless of whether the child receives treatment aimed at curing the disease. Access to palliative care is considered a fundamental human right, and all individuals, regardless of income, disease type, or age, should have access to a nationally determined set of basic health services, including palliative care. Globally, it is estimated that 40-60% of all deaths require palliative care. This care is needed for patients with a wide range of life-limiting health conditions, including cancer, AIDS, cardiovascular diseases, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, kidney failure, chronic liver disease, neurological diseases, dementia, congenital anomalies, and drug-resistant tuberculosis. Children, in particular, often face a high incidence of congenital anomalies and genetic conditions, with mortality rates being highest in the neonatal period. Each year, approximately 20 million people require palliative care in the last year of their lives, with many more needing it earlier. Of these, 78% live in lowand middle-income countries, and for children, 98% of those in need reside in such settings, with nearly half living in Africa. Pain is one of the most common and severe symptoms experienced by patients in need of palliative care. Opioid analgesics are essential for managing pain and other distressing physical symptoms associated with advanced progressive conditions. For example, 80% of patients with AIDS or cancer and 67% of those with cardiovascular disease or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease experience moderate-to-severe pain at the end of their lives. However, in 2011, 83% of the world’s population lived in countries with low to nonexistent access to opioid pain relief. Psychosocial support is another critical component of palliative care. Patients with life-threatening or terminal illnesses, as well as their caregivers, often experience significant stress. Health professionals treating these patients must be adequately trained to help them manage this stress. Additionally, health systems and facilities may need to incorporate features that address other end-of-life needs, such as spiritual care, family support, legal assistance, and a supportive physical environment. The WHO emphasizes the importance of integrating palliative care into health systems as a core component of universal health coverage. This integration is explicitly recognized in the WHO Global Action Plan for the Prevention and Control of Noncommunicable Diseases (NCDs) 2013-2020 and the WHO Framework on Integrated People-Centered Services, approved at the 69th World Health Assembly in 2016. Palliative care medicines, including those for pain relief, are included in WHO’s list of essential medicines for adults and children and should be made accessible to all who need them. These medicines include both opioid and non-opioid options for pain relief, as well as treatments for the most common symptoms in palliative care. Ensuring access to palliative care is not only an ethical obligation of health systems but also a requirement under international human rights law. The right to palliative care and pain relief is recognized as part of the human right to health. Under international drug control conventions, countries have a dual obligation to ensure that controlled substances are accessible for medical purposes while protecting populations from dependence and misuse. Unfortunately, many countries have prioritized preventing abuse over ensuring access for medical purposes. This guide serves as an operational manual for setting up palliative care services and integrating them into health systems. It outlines general principles and core components needed to strengthen palliative care and provides a range of possible starting points for establishing such services. The manual emphasizes a stepwise approach, particularly for lowand middle-income settings, and aims to promote equitable access to high-quality palliative care in the context of universal health coverage. It is designed to address patients’ needs and expectations through people-centered care, involving healthcare workers, patients, and their communities in a proactive manner that considers social and cultural specificities. While this manual does not include clinical guidelines or protocols for patient care, it references existing WHO guidance on pain and symptom management and provides a list of additional tools and resources. In the future, this manual is expected to be complemented by publications addressing more specific aspects of palliative care and additional measurement tools to monitor the quality of palliative care at the country level. Access to palliative care has been identified as a fundamental right, and WHO reaffirms its commitment to working with Member States to ensure that this becomes a reality for everyone—adults, older people, and children.
